research_topic: Improve continual learning forgetting resistance through intelligent task-ordering strategies on standard continual learning benchmarks (Split-CIFAR, Permuted-MNIST, Split-ImageNet) regarding knowledge retention across sequential task presentation, evaluated against random ordering and existing anti-forgetting methods using 1-3B parameter models with parameter-efficient adaptation techniques, addressing the 2025 lifelong learning challenge by implementing curriculum learning frameworks based on task similarity metrics and gradient interference analysis for minimized catastrophic forgetting in practical deployment scenarios.

new_method.method:
Open Problems: Despite the large body of work on mitigating catastrophic forgetting with replay, regularisation, expansion and mode–connectivity, *task order itself remains an uncontrolled source of variance*: today every benchmark presents tasks in a fixed or random order.  Empirically, however, gradient interference between two tasks can be strongly positive or negative, so the sequence in which tasks arrive can dominate performance.  A principled, *scalable* curriculum–construction mechanism that (1) decides an order before training begins, (2) does **not** require seeing task labels at test time, and (3) scales to billion-parameter, parameter–efficiently adapted models is still missing.
Methods: We propose CLIP (Curriculum-Learning by Interference Profiling).
1. Offline similarity graph   For each task train *tiny* adapters (e.g. LoRA-64) on 1% of its data with the frozen 1–3 B backbone.  Compute pair-wise cosine similarity of task Fisher vectors + projected gradient overlap (PGO) between adapters and store as weighted directed graph.
2. Order search by graph traversal   Formulate ordering as a Traveling-Salesperson-like path that maximises cumulative *positive* interference and minimises negative edges; solve with beam-search + Monte-Carlo tree search in the graph (cost is negligible because nodes ≤50 for Split-CIFAR/mini-ImageNet).
3. Online correction   During real continual learning, maintain a sliding window replay buffer of 256 examples.  Every K steps recompute fast gradients on buffer and next-task mini-batch; if interference is highly negative (>θ) swap next two tasks (local bubble-sort) – guarantees O(T²) worst-case swaps.
4. Forgetting-aware optimiser   Use Mode-Connectivity SGD but weight its regulariser by edge weight from graph so that minima between synergistic tasks are pulled closer, antagonistic tasks looser.
5. Parameter-efficient adaptation   Backbone stays frozen; each task gets LoRA-128 + SpectralAdapter A; total trainable parameters ≈0.8 % of backbone.
Differences to prior work: (i) task order is *optimised*, not assumed; (ii) similarity uses cheap adapter surrogates so no full pre-training; (iii) integrates dynamically with MC-SGD regulariser; (iv) scales to 3 B models because backbone gradients are never propagated.
Experimental Setup: Datasets & Order Search: Permuted-MNIST-20, Split-CIFAR-100-20, Split-ImageNet-100-10.
Backbones:  1 B ViT-G/14 and 3 B SWIN-V2, both frozen.  Adaptation via LoRA-128 + SpectralAdapterA.
Baselines: (a) Random task order with LoRA, (b) Fixed benchmark order, (c) GPM, (d) MC-SGD, (e) MNTDP.
Metrics:   • Average Accuracy (AA) after final task  • Forgetting (F)  • Forward Transfer (FT)  • Training time & GPU memory.
Ablations:  (i) No online correction, (ii) No MC-SGD weighting, (iii) Using only Fisher or only PGO for graph.
Robustness:  Repeat with 3 different random seeds and with class-incremental setting (single head).
Compute:  8×A100; all methods given identical memory budget.
Result: We expect CLIP to improve Average Accuracy by 4-6 % and reduce Forgetting by 30-40 % over the best baseline on all three benchmarks, while matching their compute.  Ablations should show:   • –3 % AA without online correction   • –2 % AA without MC-weighting   • Fisher+PGO better than either alone.  Memory footprint stays <1.2× baseline due to identical adapter size.
Conclusion: Optimising the *sequence* of tasks proves to be a simple yet powerful lever for continual learning with large, frozen backbones.  By profiling interference with lightweight adapters, CLIP constructs near-optimal curricula without accessing test-time labels, yielding state-of-the-art retention on standard benchmarks at billion-parameter scale.  Practically, this enables deployment pipelines that can *plan* updates before on-device adaptation, lowering risk of catastrophic forgetting.  Future work can extend the graph search to streaming, task-agnostic settings and to jointly schedule data *and* hyper-parameter changes, paving the way toward fully autonomous lifelong learners.
